They were St. Gene, they had some good ones. But they left there and went to Baton Rouge.
Who was that from St. James?
That was, uh, Clackmont. Called his name a while ago.
Is that from Donaldsonville?

That's from Donaldsonville, yeah. Old man, uh, Clayborne Williams. Yeah, that'd be Clayborne Williams. He died when his son still played. He played in Baton Rouge. But he still played Dixieland music. Clayborne? Yeah, old man Clayborne's been there.
His son plays Dixieland?

Oh yeah, he's good, good. Yeah, yeah, George. He's doing anything. When he first started playing, he was a little boy with Harvard. Uncle Luke, super big as that. Used to play that with his dad. I remember that girl.
It's the tiny boy, huh?

Yeah, his sister's playing piano. He's pretty good. He used to stop here all the time. He stopped here about 17 years. He used to play back every labor day. He played back here. And from here, they go to town and play. Go in.
Well, how old was Thomas when he started playing music?
Thomas was young. He started from me. By me having a black band, leave all the instruments here, you know. And he'd be here. Be fooling on him. Playing on him.
Right in this house? Yeah, right in this house.

He started lying there. He's working. He used to work and play music. Well, he left here. There's five minutes to spread. He's holding Ken to feed on the plantation. Throw the hole down. So I'm going home. He said, look at the next 12 o'clock. They're going to dock. He said, don't kill. He said, no more work for me. He said, but he's going to dock here. It's most 12 o'clock. I said, I don't kill. Take the hole to the house. He said, he's going to go dock him. He's gone. He left there. No more work for me. Ain't no more home. Let him dock me. The little one I got, he can take it. Stop home.
And he just quit and started playing music.

Started playing music. That's right. He played on up to the left. And the wacky used to work out on jobs in the city. Worked to the black men. I think that black men had allergies. They had better moves. And they do play a little wacky. Varnish on. Chair. All big. And paint. Little cobblers. Do a good job down there. Work for flacky. Do better jobs in the family in the city. Take more time. And do the work good. Oh, yeah. Yeah. You look just for the money. It's too color, isn't it? Yeah, it's too color. Yeah, it's too color. He's like, all right, you know.
Well, I think we're about gone off on it. Unless you wanted to ask something. I just wanted to ask you one thing. Where do you think the idea of having bands at funerals came from?
What's that?
Where do you think the idea of having bands at funerals came from? Because...

I don't know. I wouldn't know. I know it was here all the way it was. And they stopped it because they were so sad, you know. Band would be out there on the grave, on the grave frame, you know, the funeral home. And the relationship would be hard and can't on the dragon. Well, I know it was something way back years ago, that they said a funeral was so sad, till somebody got the idea of, like a society, and said, well, hard music, but they got to play hymns behind them. Yeah. Now, after they got that, and everybody would be happy coming back, but they just got the idea of playing something hot and coming back. Yeah, playing all the... Fancy. Fancy. Fancy. Most times they would play for guys who'd play in the band. Yeah. Yeah. You know, you know. They had music at it. They would die when they played at funerals. That's where I heard it. Yeah.
Because it's something that's so different in this part of the country, you know, from anywhere else. Yeah.
Why you from, you from a foreign, I know you from up north somewhere.
No, I'm, well, I was born in the north, but I've lived in New Orleans most of my life. Oh, I see.

Um... Well, they used to like that, but they cut it out after the band, whatever, all the distance, and had many brass bands. And when all the fellas that used to play, they all died, some left here, and... Wasn't much here, so we didn't want to get a dollar to walk about, what, 10 miles. She wasn't walking all right. Well, what, 10 miles for a dollar. 10 miles for a dollar. That's right. She all night started dancing. What time did we start dancing? Seven o'clock or eight o'clock? Seven o'clock. Seven o'clock. Seven o'clock. Seven o'clock. Eight o'clock. Well, they played at four o'clock. Four o'clock in the morning. Seven o'clock in the morning. Seven o'clock in the morning. Sometimes a man would make enough money to pay you. They don't pay the four hours, no. Yeah, the four hours. You get about fifteen, twenty dollars or something. Well, you see, after it started getting union fee. Yeah. It's changing all that dollars. Change, yeah. It's changing. Yeah, you know. What, you used to kill? You don't know Mr. Marshall? Yeah, I told him I'll carry around.
We don't go by there in a while.
Yeah, I told him I'll carry around over there.
Did they have many city bands come out here?
No, not much. A little bit of bands, like I tell you, they come out sometime.
Which one is that?

I mean, the fella I told you, he used to come out so often, but I don't sense. He needed to cut him out. And you don't care what's coming out. He's a big man. I ain't make plenty of money in the union. He's called Dave, yeah.
Dave Bartholomew, but I mean in the old days. Oh, the old days. Oh, yeah.
He's always having.
Yeah. 된 stuff with

city bands would come out here? Let's see. Robichaud used to come out here. John Robichaud? The violin player? Yeah, the violin player. I mean the violin player, left-handed. Yeah, really good. Well they only had bass and trumpet and that's like we talked, that's all he used to have. Short band? Yeah, he had no drum at that time. And I'd be, I think I'd find out, I can't call his name, I'd find out me to come out here. But Rubichaud used to be more so popular than the others. Always have old Matt Martin, he had no good you know, he liked Rubichaud.
Well I think we better get on up the road and see your friend, we should appreciate this. Yeah, you got it for me, just me.
Yeah, I got you. stuff

segments.title: Recording opening: name, home and place (Reserve)
segments.summary: Zander gets Valentine's full name, introduces the people present, and notes the recording is at his home in Reserve.

segments.title: Birthplace, age and date of recording
segments.summary: Valentine says he was born in Reserve, married at about 17, and is around 80; the date is given as June 24, 1960.

segments.title: Pickwick Brass Band: Jim Humphrey's lessons and the first members
segments.summary: He recalls the brass band in Reserve that Jim Humphrey came to teach on Sundays, and begins naming its twelve members, Gus Macchette and Joe Stewart on tuba.

segments.title: Dejan, how Valentine met him, and more band members
segments.summary: He names Dejan on trumpet, tells how they met when his family moved from Raceland to Reserve, and lists August, Piton and Hoes on clarinet.

segments.title: Drummers Noonell Thomas and Son Mason, and Marshall Lawrence's string band
segments.summary: He adds drummers Noonell Thomas and Son Mason and describes Marshall Lawrence, a violinist with his own string band.

segments.title: Band instrumentation: altos, trombones, E-flat trumpet, Sammy Robins
segments.summary: They tally the instruments, two altos including Ernest Martin, two trombones, clarinets, no saxophones, an E-flat horn, and trumpeter Sammy Robins.

segments.title: Learning music from Dejan and playing other instruments
segments.summary: He had no formal teacher and learned from Dejan, who taught the whole band; he played some trumpet but tried every instrument.

segments.title: Earlier La Place brass bands: Vance, George Treacher
segments.summary: He names older brass band players from La Place, including Vance, a string bass player, and George Treacher.

segments.title: Pickwick and La Place bands, grandson Joseph, church and hymns
segments.summary: He names the band and its Sunday meetings with La Place bands, then talks about his pianist grandson Joseph, his Baptist and Catholic upbringing, and bands playing for churches.

segments.title: Where bands played, societies, pay and prices
segments.summary: Bands played in halls and parades for societies; pay was around twelve dollars for the band or less, and he recalls how far a dime or nickel went.

segments.title: Funerals with the band, second line, Catholics and Baptists
segments.summary: They played funerals like New Orleans, with hymns going out and hot music coming back, and played for both Catholic and Baptist societies.

segments.title: Attempt to get a family member to play; light and eyesight
segments.summary: Zander asks to hear someone play; there is hesitation, talk about reading music and poor light, and the recording is paused.

segments.title: Reading music and the repertoire for parades, dances and funerals
segments.summary: He says the bandsmen mostly played by ear or what they were shown, with Dejan a good reader; marches and hymns were used at funerals but not at dances.

segments.title: Musicians from the neighborhood: Hall Boys, Herb Tree, Marshall
segments.summary: He names musicians from the area, including the Hall Boys, Kid Ory, and George Tree's son Herb, a saxophonist in California who played with Marshall.

segments.title: His son Freddie and the music they play
segments.summary: Zander meets his son, who plays rock and roll, a bit of Dixieland, and has sung in school opera.

segments.title: Best clarinet and trumpet players: Doc Feller Thomas, Dejan
segments.summary: He names Doc Feller Thomas as a fine clarinetist who played with his son, and Dejan as the best trumpeter and best by ear.

segments.title: Manuel Perez, Buddy Bolden and the country bands' rivalry with the city
segments.summary: Asked about Perez and Bolden, he did not see them play but says city people ranked his band the best.

segments.title: Dixieland, quadrilles, and brass and string band instrumentation
segments.summary: He says Dixieland was always played, by the same bands that played quadrilles, and describes brass bands and string bands with no drums at dances.

segments.title: When pianos arrived and six-piece dance bands
segments.summary: Pianos came late, around when drums did, and the dance bands he played with were six pieces without piano.

segments.title: Edward Clem, Tig Chambers, Manuel Manetta and Clayborne Williams
segments.summary: Questions about various musicians: Edward Clem of St. James, Tig Chambers, a two-horn teacher, and the Clayborne Williams family of Donaldsonville who played Dixieland.

segments.title: Kid Thomas starts playing at home and quits plantation work
segments.summary: His son Thomas began on instruments left in the house, then walked off a plantation job to play music full time.

segments.title: Origin of bands at funerals
segments.summary: He does not know where the custom came from but recalls the idea of hymns going to the grave and hot music coming back to cheer people.

segments.title: Decline of the brass bands, long walks and union pay
segments.summary: The brass bands faded as players died or left; he recalls walking ten miles for a dollar, all-night dances, and pay changing once the union came.

segments.title: City bands visiting and closing
segments.summary: He recalls city bands that came out to Reserve, especially left-handed violinist John Robichaud's small group, then Zander wraps up to visit another friend.
